title: A demo menu — scripted walkthroughs that are simultaneously a tutorial, a review tool, and a real-server integration test
summary: A big, obvious button opening a menu of named demos (e.g. 'The GM Process'). Picking one runs a scripted, step-by-step macro against the REAL live module and the REAL local Foundry server — never mocked — narrating what a GM or player would do at each step and driving the actual UI to do it. Triples as: a tutorial for a new user, Ingram's fast lane to trying and critiquing a UI flow end to end, and a real-server test that anything broken breaks loudly during the demo itself.
description:
Ingram's own framing, captured close to verbatim (2026-09-17, mid-session on the deck rebuild): 'create a system for demos... a nice big obvious button to access a menu of possible demos... shows off how a UI element works by going through a macro that acts like a tutorial AND also allows me to experience your UI/UX work directly. Anything which breaks should break during the demo because we always run real commands on the real server to prove our process is a good one that works... a very long demo called "The GM Process" which shows how the GM would go through the story one step at a time and show off what the UI would help them do at each step... a tutorial and test AND a way for me to try out your ideas, critique them and then get the same experience again +/- my suggested changes. This allows us to walk through the entire experience of using the UI which gives me a fast track to debugging and helping design the UX.'

**Why this is more than a nice-to-have, and worth its own real design pass rather than a quick bolt-on:** it directly answers this session's own recurring cost — every UI change in this project currently gets verified by hand, one Browser-pane click sequence at a time, re-derived fresh each session (see reference_local_foundry_test_environment). A scripted, replayable demo is that same verification work, captured once and made replayable by anyone (Claude in a future session, or Ingram herself), AND it is the fastest possible loop for the exact iterative-review style already established as this project's working pattern (feedback_iterative_visual_review: get something real on screen, react to it in short terms, re-run to confirm the correction landed). 'Same experience again +/- my suggested changes' is literally re-running the demo after an edit — which this project already does by hand, constantly, throughout this very session.

**The 'never mocked' constraint is the load-bearing design decision.** A demo step is not a scripted animation or a canned screenshot — it is a real macro issuing real actions against the real live module and a real Foundry world (create/select a token, click the actual deck control, post the actual chat message, advance the actual day-ring setting), the same way this session's own live-verification passes already work, just captured as a replayable script instead of ad hoc tool calls. If a step's target element has moved, been renamed, or the underlying system has drifted, the demo throws or visibly stalls at exactly that step — which is the point: 'anything which breaks should break during the demo.'

**Relationship to existing testing tiers, worth being precise about:** design/testing-strategy.md's tiers (0-4) test CODE — pure logic, contracts, mocked adapters. This is a different, additive thing: a scripted END-TO-END walkthrough of USER-FACING FLOW, closer in spirit to the battle-simulator's real-dice, real-rules-engine philosophy (tools/battle-simulator/) than to a unit test, but for the UI instead of combat math. It would not replace any existing tier — a demo breaking tells you the FLOW broke, not which function; the existing tiers still own root-causing it once flagged.

**A concrete shape worth recording, not committing to:** a demo is a named, ordered list of steps, each step pairing (a) a narrated line of what a GM/player is doing and why, written in the GM-facing prose style this project already keeps to (feedback_gm_facing_prose_style — plain instructional sentences, no aphorism), and (b) the real action to perform (a DOM interaction on the real rendered deck, or a direct call to the same adapter function a click would trigger) plus what to check afterward before calling the step done. A menu (the 'big obvious button') lists demos by name; running one narrates each step, pauses or highlights the element in question (echoing 'shows off how a UI element works'), and only advances once the step's own check confirms the real state actually changed. Whether narration is passive (auto-advancing with a pause) or Ingram clicks 'next' herself is an open question below, as is whether steps are skippable/replayable individually rather than only as one continuous run.

**Not started.** Ingram was explicit: capture this as a tracked objective, do not build it now. This entry exists so it is not rediscovered from scratch whenever it does become the right thing to pick up.

**Update, 2026-09-18 — greenlit and built, as the proof for that same day's integration pass.** Asked directly whether to build this now, given how close it sits to what proving a large integration pass actually works would need anyway, Ingram chose "build it as the integration's proof." `module/blank-inheritance/scripts/core/demo.mjs` (the pure walk — which step, can it advance/retreat, shape validation) already existed as an untracked skeleton from earlier the same day; `module/blank-inheritance/scripts/foundry/demo-runner.mjs` now adds the Foundry-touching half this entry's own open questions left unanswered, resolving them by example rather than by further design: a demo is hand-authored JS (not a declarative DSL — the simpler of the two named options), GM-paced with a Next/Back per step, runs against whichever world is actually open (no disposable per-run world), and is one continuous walk with no per-step replay yet. The 'big obvious button' is a GM macro (`createDemoMacroIfMissing`, same idiom as the Director's Panel and Scene Set macros) opening a small toggle panel styled like the City Board/Summon Panel, listing demos by name (DEMOS is an array for exactly the 'menu of possible demos' reason, even with one entry today).

The one demo built, `session-01-integration`, proves the day's whole integration end to end against REAL Episode One content: opens the Scene Runner on the Road In, picks and cuts to Kit Issue (a different real location, so the map-travel ritual fires), stages Kit Issue's Nobu (a real cast member already authored with `arrival: "announced"`, so the automatic sting-tier wiring fires for real), repeats the crossing to Canteen, stages Canteen's Taka (`arrival: "splash"`, the loudest tier), and opens the Sound Desk from the Deck's own new Sound pill. Every step either calls the exact function a macro click would use or clicks a real button on the real rendered Scene Runner/Deck — never a mock — and throws if its target element or expected end state doesn't show up, which is this idea's own load-bearing design decision working as intended. Not yet run for real against a live Foundry world; see the parent integration effort's own live-verification pass.
sourceContext: Mid-session on the deck rebuild, immediately after a round of live UI feedback (grime tuning, hiding the native player roster, the hotbar rampart, the scene-runner drawer). Ingram explicitly said not to implement yet and to track it as an objective for whenever it seems best to start.
openSubQuestions: How much of 'The GM Process' (the worked example named directly) would double-cover ground design/scene-simulation-testing.md's self-play protocol (issue #137) already covers from a different angle — that protocol predicts outcomes and cross-checks against a live UI run too. Worth reading that doc first when this is picked up, to reuse rather than duplicate its own real-server-verification discipline. Not investigated when the first demo was built 2026-09-18 — 'The GM Process' itself is not the demo that shipped.

Does a broken demo step get filed as a GitHub issue automatically (matching feedback_github_tracker_discipline's 'log it in the same turn' rule), or does surfacing it live to Ingram in the moment count as the loud failure the design already wants? Not decided — the shipped runner just shows the error in its own panel and stops; nothing files an issue automatically yet.
resolvedSubQuestions: Script format, resolved 2026-09-18 by building it: hand-authored JS per demo, not a declarative DSL — `module/blank-inheritance/scripts/foundry/demo-runner.mjs`'s own DEMOS array, one plain object literal per demo.
Pacing, resolved 2026-09-18: GM-paced, a Next/Back click per step, matching design/ux-doctrine.md's 'judgement is never automated' reasoning and how Ingram already reviews UI work.
World, resolved 2026-09-18: runs against whichever world is actually open, not a disposable per-run world — no throwaway-world machinery was built.
Replay, resolved 2026-09-18 (for now): one continuous run start to finish, no per-step skip/replay yet.
resolution: 2026-09-18: a first demo (session-01-integration) is built and wired into the module (mounted panel, GM macro, module API), proving that same day's Scene Runner / map-travel / automatic-sting-tier / Deck integration end to end against real Episode One content. Not yet run live against a real Foundry world. The fuller vision (a declarative script format, per-step replay, a disposable throwaway world, automatic issue-filing on a broken step) remains open — this is Layer 0 of the idea, not the whole thing.
